The test image shows a tomato stem at or near the soil line with prominent white cottony mycelium and what appear to be dark sclerotia embedded in it. The stem is rotting and the plant appears wilted. Top candidates: **Southern_Blight** (Sclerotium rolfsii - white mycelium + small round sclerotia at soil line) and **Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot** (white mycelium + larger black sclerotia).

Let me view reference images for these top candidates, then explore others.
Interesting - the test image has Bugwood ID 5593845, and this Sclerotinia reference is 5593847 (very close). Let me check more Sclerotinia references.

The Southern_Blight_23 close-up shows white mycelium with small round sclerotia on a stem - very similar to the test image. I've covered 2 classes with 6 views. I need 2 more views from different classes to meet the 8-class requirement.

Gray Mold affects fruit (not matching), and Alternaria shows dark stem cankers (no mycelium). Neither matches the test image.

**Analysis summary:**

Test image key features:
- Tomato stem at soil line with white cottony mycelium
- Dark nodular sclerotia embedded in the white growth
- Stem decay/rot visible; plant wilting above
- Black plastic mulch in background, soil context

**Visual comparison:**
- **Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot** (Bugwood_2, ID 5593847): Same field setting with black plastic mulch, same plant wilting pattern. Critically, the test image Bugwood ID is 5593845 — just 2 numbers away, strongly indicating same photographer/disease series. Sclerotinia produces white cottony mycelium with larger, irregular, darkening sclerotia.
- **Southern_Blight** (Bugwood_23): Close-up shows white mycelium + small sclerotia on stem — visually similar too, but sclerotia in S. rolfsii are small, round, and tan/brown (mustard-seed sized). The dark, larger, more irregular structures in the test image lean Sclerotinia.

The Bugwood ID proximity (5593845 vs 5593847) and the bleached/white stem tissue with dark irregular sclerotia in white cottony mycelium align more with Sclerotinia Timber Rot.

The sclerotia appear larger and darker than the small round tan sclerotia typical of Southern Blight (Sclerotium rolfsii), and the bleached stem tissue fits Sclerotinia better.
